Search & Rescue: The art of finding a missing person or criminal

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Did you kn0w that a missing person acts a specific way? We take you on a wild ride to find out about the dogs and their handlers searching to find missing people and criminals.

Unique Selling Point:
Missing Person Behaviour

John Traas a scientist and search and rescue expert knows the behaviour of a missing person. So much so that before they even call in the dogs, he's often able to help volunteers locate the person. Through extensive research and in speaking to renowned experts around the world he's now been able to collate his knowledge and has come up with a scientific paper regarding the what a missing person does based on their age, sex, disability etc For example: A 10 year old child will react differently to a 4 year old. A person with Dimentia reacts differently than a person with autism. A middle aged man, reacts different to a teen female. This has become a guide for search and rescue personnel around the world. And is being used as an application in today's missing person's searches right her in South Africa. They are located around the country, a lot in Cape Town obviously.

Summary:
But there are different versions of search and rescue dogs as well = like an air scenter - which works off leash, and used to cover larger spaces more rapidly to narrow a search area and then mantrailing dogs, which will literally track the air clouds that come off of the missing person directly to where they have gone. These are the new types of dogs that now do search and rescue. We no longer use tracking dogs because they take too long and go along the literal path or every foot print - it takes hours, where as air scenters and mantrailers can take minutes, and mantrailers can track a scent hours and day old. Jackie de Souza is the only person in Africa who been trained in mantrailing by the INBTI - International Bloodhound Training institute. She works in South Africa and Swaziland, but is contracted around Africa to teach. She has been contracted by the Swaziland police to track criminals for them... so much so that criminals often just hand themselves over than be hunted by her team. Amazing video of this! What we have learned is that dogs will track the freshest and most interesting scent, meaning that tricky criminals cant outdo the dogs - whether its going through water, driving off in a car, trying to mask your scent.... the dogs will find them...

Further information:
also interesting: criminals often have a "fear" pheromone that is like a red line of "follow me" for dogs. Robyn Hartflett can also explain how scent works in dogs, she and her team of search and rescuers have gone on table mountain and saved many hikers or found bodies etc she is an air scenting expert. https://www.pressreader.com/south-africa/pretoria-news-weekend/20141108/281788512345168

Extra Budget Items:
One day in cape town to film to interview Traas and the search and rescue team. We will need a drone.

Script:


(see mac putting on ghillie suit) No I’m not heading off to war…
but I am trying to outwit a fierce adversary … (see nose, paws, tail then reveal dog, panting sounds...)
SOUNDUP: MAC ATTACK COMMENT
But before I unleash my full Mac Attack let’s take a step back - and enter a world in which canine is King...
Dogs are genetically programmed to hunt. It’s this innate ability that handlers develop in order to track a humans. But just like every man can run, not everyone can run an ultra marathon… It's the same here, these are no ordinary pets, but highly trained working breeds; some track footprints or scent the air while others trail the freshest clouds of scent molecules people leave behind. A person on the move leaves behind a trail of scent molecules on the ground and in the air. Dogs trained to follow this odour are called mantrailers.
Mike: if she’s now the dog and she’s busy going out, I let the line go through my fingers like that...
Michael Capazorio is an assistant mantrailing trainer practising out of Lonehill, Johannesburg. He showed me how to handle Kipling, a one year-old border collie.
[ACTION UPSOUND OF MICHAEL SHOWING MAC]
“Check”
We are telling Kipling that the scent underneath his harness is his target scent. He then walks a circle, eliminating all the non-target scents, before we set off. In no time, he has found his mark. (THE REST OF THE SOUNDUP FROM MICHAEL)
It is used by us for search and rescue and for trying to apprehend criminals. The dog following the odour of the specific person we asked him to go after.
Man-trailing is relatively new and Jackie de Sousa is one of only a handful of qualified trainers in Africa. De Sousa began work with the Swaziland police force, helping them track arsonists.
J: They had a 75% drop in the arson fires because of the dogs finding them. we are standing over 600 successful missions. That means that other the missing person has been found, or the criminal has been apprehended, arrested, convicted.
Mac: What would you say has been the oldest trail that your dogs have picked up?
J: We had a blood hound that trailed a three week old trail.
Kipling’s owner Caroline Howes has found the change in her dog miraculous - before channeling his energy into this training, he was not a happy puppy.
CH: So he is an incredibly driven working dog, he was bred to work 10 hours aday out on a sheep dog working, so this lets him use his brain and body together and it really makes him tired. No don’t lick the lens! It makes me happy to see him happy.
And if you think you can escape by running through water, think again.
M: So if the scent has dropped around me while I'm moving through the water, the dogs can pick up the scent that has fallen down.
But hunting down criminals is not the only use for these canine noses. A beautiful day out hiking in the mountains can turn treacherous when bad weather rolls in unexpectedly. Before you know it you’re lost or injured. Search and rescue operations - manned by mountain club volunteers, paramedics and dog handlers like the crew from the Western Cape’s K9 Search and Rescue Association - often mean the difference between life and death.
The thing with search and rescue is that most of the time you don’t find a living patient, and that is the reality of it.
Veteran handler, Lita Potgieter and her border collie, Chase are always primed to go out. Chase is an air-scenter, trained to scan vast areas for the presence of a human. He works off-leash to make the most of his four-legged speed.
They just looking for a living human scent. We search only for the missing person in that area. Your smell is drifting on the air in a certain direction and as they go across that smell, they realize ooo that’s the smell that I'm looking for.
The outcome, though, often isn’t a happy one as Potgieter and fellow wilderness first responder James Smart know all too well. Led by Smart’s Belgian Shepherd, jedi, they once continued searching for a missing child at the point others might have called off the operation.
So there was some kids playing in a tunnel, and the tunnel collapsed. they’d already pulled two of the kids out of the tunnel, but they now not sure how many more or where they are So they bought Jedi in and he indicated in the sand, too. And I said the child is there. And he indicated again, he actually started digging himself in the sand. and I think another four or five meters in there actually found the fourth child.
Unfortunately, the children had been crushed in the collapse and none survived.
Its very traumatic for our dogs when they experience that cos they are trained on live scent… this dog was depressed for 4 days afterwards he was still not himself.
As well as an art, search and rescue is a passion... but it’s also becoming a science. Local search and rescue legend John Traas believes recovery can become supercharged by studying the behaviour of people who’ve previously gone missing.
Any stats that were kept to describe what missing people had done or lost people had done, they started picking up patterns
The patterns are drawn from the statistics of people of different age groups who've gone missing while doing a range of activities, like hunting or hiking.
All it tells you is where people likely have in the past been found, how long they've survived in the past, how far have they travelled.I f you look at a sort of 1-3 toddler, first thing you need to do is find out is there any water? (delete) Because little kids are drawn to swimming pools
The data shows that even when dealing with mental illness, people follow certain patterns when lost.
if a dementia patient leaves a care facility. They will keep walking in a straight line. from that door until they can't go any further. And there have been a number of cases of particularly Alzheimer sufferers found literally hung up in a thorn bush So they're just stop there and wait till somebody finds.
Today, it’s best practice to combine the data with the dogs’s innate abilities to maximise the odds for experienced search and rescue operators.
Much younger children will look for some way to settle in where they're safe, they'll crawl under a log, and often go to sleep. Which is of course where dogs become so useful because the dog isn't listening for the child, the dog is using his nose,
And the new science of mantrailing makes the process even quicker and more efficient. Unlike tracking dogs, mantrailers don’t stick to the spoor, but take the shortest route to where the scent is freshest, ignoring places where the target circles or backtracks. These dogs execute pursuits of stunning complexity. Watch as these two dogs chase down suspects that have escaped from a stolen vehicle.
You have chased the vehicle, managed to pull it off the road, and the ppl bailout say there were 4 int vehicle and you manage to catch two, two has gotten away.
The first dog goes into the car and picks up the scents of all four suspects. Then he eliminates the two who have already been caught. Now he indicates the trail of the two fugitives. He and his handler set off after one of the fleeing suspects. The second dog does the same - but she can tell where her canine colleague has gone. She automatically chooses the second trail. Both suspects are chased down and caught...But is the same in store for me? It was time to put my camouflage - and wits - to the test.
SOUNDUPS
Yolan Friedman and her 10 month old Belgian Shepherd Malinois called Viper are up for my challenge…
SOUNDUPS
…Even our camera man found it hard work to keep up with the dog… (falls) But Viper totally outwitted me.
Tracking isn’t for all dogs or handlers. For it to work, a dog must have a high drive and be of medium size. It mustn't be aggressive or wary of humans. In the end it’s up to the handler to read their dog and hone science with experience and the age-old instincts of man’s best friend.
J: It's like a umbilical cord that line between, like you have with a mom and a baby you have between the dog and that's that sensitivity of a handler getting his dog in the dog getting the handler there's nothing that can substitute for that.
